Rhizoma Smoke holds the SG Rhizoma Engine, the Sativus Gourd atelier’s growth engine, and the SG Rhizoma Typeface Family grown with it, led by SG Smoke, the face that gives the page its name. The engine is built on Rhizoma, Dabin Kim’s growing type system for the letters of IM Fell English, and adds Hangul, smoke that climbs out of the letter, roots that join across letters and lines, growth that rises through a text, and seeds that bring any growth back.

01Constant ConnectionRoots that join across letters and lines.
중심 뿌리나 명확한 경계가 없는 이 생장 방식은 디지털 경험을 설명하는 완벽한 은유다.“A rhizome, which spreads horizontally without a central root or clear boundaries, serves as a perfect metaphor for the modern digital experience of infinite connection and entanglement.”Dabin Kim, Rhizoma

In botany, a rhizome is an underground stem that spreads sideways and sprouts new roots at every node. The idea goes back to Deleuze and Guattari’s A Thousand Plateaus, where “any point of a rhizome can be connected to anything other, and must be.”

Rhizoma takes the first half of that sentence. Its roots spread from every letter and cross one another, but each grows from one point to one tip and passes over the rest. The SG Rhizoma Engine takes the second half: in SG Drag and SG Tangle, a root that comes near another root, letter or line joins it, so a word grows as one body and two lines as one field.

02Gradual ProliferationGrowth that rises letter by letter, and fonts with a Growth axis.

Rhizoma grows every letter of a text at the same growth stage and line weight. In Kim’s zine, a spread of text grows denser from one page to the next, and one A grows through rising stages. Here growth can change along a text: Growth, in the SG Rhizoma Engine at the top, sets it where the text starts and where it ends, on Rhizoma’s own scale of 0 to 20. SG Rhizoma V2 follows that scale exactly. The other faces are fitted to it: 10 is each face as its font grows it, and each grows as one plant, so a step up keeps every root of the step below and adds more. At 20, SG Smoke climbs to a forest of separate stems and SG Drag puts its growth into the current, with more strands and longer drifts. SG Roses leaves its line and spreads until the letters are lost in it, as they are in SG Rhizoma V2.

A font cannot know where a letter sits on a page, so every core face also comes as a variable font: SG Smoke, SG Roses, SG Drag and SG Rhizoma V2, and SG Flame among the experiments. Their Growth axis runs from the bare letter at 0 to the full growth at 100 and can be set per word, line or page in any app that reads variable fonts.

04How a Letter GrowsFrom an IM Fell English glyph to one grown outline.

The letter is IM Fell English, Igino Marini’s digitisation of the Fell Types, the founts Bishop John Fell left to Oxford in 1686: Dutch-model romans older than Caslon. Marini kept the uneven edges and ink spread of the printed page, so the letter looks grown before a single root appears.

Rhizoma’s growing type system grows in five moves: it scatters points inside the letter, lets a few of them sprout, walks each root forward in small random turns, lets roots branch, and fuses roots and letter into one outline, ready to save as a font or a vector file.

Every face here makes those five moves. SG Rhizoma V2 makes them as the original does, at the default settings. The other faces vary in where a root sprouts, how it walks, and whether it joins what it meets. The R below is SG Roses: its roots start on the outline and leave along the outward normal, straight out of the letter.

06Hangul / 한글The 2,350 syllables of KS X 1001, every one of them grown.

For an atelier that works in Korean as often as English, Hangul was the first addition. The SG Rhizoma Engine reads two typefaces as one stack: Latin from IM Fell English and Hangul from Song Myung, an open-source Myeongjo, the Korean serif tradition. A syllable block holds far more ink than a Latin letter, so every face but SG Rhizoma V2 sprouts Hangul at 0.45 of the Latin rate, and a line of Hangul grows about as densely as a line of Latin.

Hangul’s distinctions are small. One short stroke separates ㅏ from ㅑ, and a tick on top turns ㅈ into ㅊ. A root that leaves a stem in the wrong place can read as a stroke. The lower sprout rate is the first guard: fewer roots per syllable leaves fewer chances to land on a stem. The second is direction. In SG Flame, roots sprout only from edges that face upward and then rise, so no root starts on the side of a vertical stem, where ㅏ would turn into ㅑ and ㅓ into ㅕ.

The third is a guard in SG Roses, where every root starts on the outline of a stroke. Once a line has grown, it takes out any Hangul root that leaves its syllable sideways, where the tick of ㅏ or ㅓ sits, and any root whose part outside the letter is short and nearly straight, the tick that turns ㅡ into ㅗ or ㅈ into ㅊ. Every other root stays where it grew, Latin is untouched, and the SG Roses font carries the same guard.

Special Thanks to Dabin Kim

The SG Rhizoma Engine is built upon Rhizoma, the growing type system Dabin Kim released openly under a CC BY-SA 4.0 licence, and every face on this page grows by her method. Her zine of the same name, in Korean and English, describes the system.

SG Smoke stays closest to the original: the same sampling and walk, with fewer roots that taper, drift upward and break up as they climb. SG Rhizoma V2 is the original engine at its default settings, with seeds, Hangul, growth that can rise through a text, and fonts that install with kerning and ligatures, one of them with a Growth axis.
